items.statement:
Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, no closed components, and supplied radial collars. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint isolated smooth arcs $A_j$ with distinct endpoints on $L$. Each is the radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior, and the two transverse boundary-curve crossings at its ends have equal ordered signs on the boundary tori oriented outward toward the exterior. No intersection circles occur. Suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_0;\mathbb Z)+\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_1;\mathbb Z)$.

For every open neighborhood $N$ of $L\cup\bigcup_j A_j$ there is a continuous surjection $Q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $N$, whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the $A_j$, such that $Q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ smooth embedded two-spheres. Each sphere contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The assertion allows disconnected or nonorientable spanning surfaces and an empty arc list. It does not assert that $Q$ is smooth, recover an alternating diagram, or identify the quotient graph $Q(L)$ with the original link.

citations.quote:
Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded surfaces with the same nonempty boundary link $L$, with no closed components and with supplied radial collars around $L$. Suppose their entire intersection is $L$ together with $n$ pairwise disjoint smooth arcs $A_1,\ldots,A_n$ whose distinct endpoints lie on $L$. Each arc is the isolated radial extension of a proper transverse common arc in the link exterior; the two boundary curves on the surrounding tori cross transversely at its endpoints, with equal ordered intersection signs when the tori are oriented outward toward the exterior. Thus every arc is standard. No intersection circles occur.

Write $b_i=\operatorname{rank}H_1(F_i;\mathbb Z)$ and suppose $c(F_0)=c(F_1)=p$ and $n=b_0+b_1$. There is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$ whose only nonsingleton fibers are exactly the arcs $A_j$, supported in any prescribed disjoint neighborhoods of those arcs. Its image $S=q(F_0\cup F_1)$ is a disjoint union of exactly $p$ locally flat embedded topological two-spheres. Each component of $S$ contains the images of exactly one component of each $F_i$. The conclusion includes $n=0$ and allows nonorientable or disconnected spanning surfaces. It does not assert smoothness of these quotient spheres or reconstruct a link diagram.

For a supplied smooth embedded arc $A\subset S^3$ and any neighborhood $U$ of it, there is a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off a smooth closed ball $B\subset U$ and on a neighborhood of $\partial B$, whose only nonsingleton fiber is $A$. It preserves $B$, and its restriction
$$q:S^3\setminus A\longrightarrow S^3\setminus\{q(A)\}$$
is a smooth diffeomorphism. No choice axiom is required.

More explicitly, in any supplied smooth chart with $A=[-1,1]\times\{0,0\}$, take the outer confocal ellipsoid with semiaxes $\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2},\varepsilon,\varepsilon$ inside that chart. The collapse may be chosen to send its smaller confocal level of parameter $\rho$ to the ellipsoid with semiaxes $f(\rho),\rho,\rho$, where $f(\rho)=a\rho$ near zero, $a>0$, and $f(\rho)=\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$ near $\varepsilon$. Thus its sufficiently small target levels are homothetic, while its formula is the identity near the outer boundary.

Assume full AC. Let $F_0,F_1\subset S^3$ be compact smooth embedded spanning surfaces for the same nonempty link $L$, with supplied radial collars in disjoint smooth normal tubes of $L$. Orient each component of $L$ arbitrarily, orient the tube boundary tori by their outward normal toward the link exterior, and orient the two surface boundary curves compatibly with $L$. Let $\alpha$ be a smooth proper transverse common arc in the exterior, transverse to its boundary, with transverse boundary-curve crossings at its distinct endpoints. Extend it radially to an isolated smooth embedded arc $A$ ending on $L$. Suppose its two ordered endpoint intersection signs agree, so their sum is $2$ or $-2$.

For every open neighborhood $U$ of $A$ there are a smooth closed ball $B\subset U$ with $A\subset\operatorname{int}B$ and a continuous surjection $q:S^3\to S^3$, fixed off $\operatorname{int}B$, such that its only non-singleton fiber is $A$, $q(B)=B$, and
$$(B,q((F_0\cup F_1)\cap B))\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\}).$$
Thus this actual local surface image is a properly embedded locally flat disk, including at the collapsed point. The surfaces may be disconnected or nonorientable. No definiteness or primeness assumption is needed for this local assertion.

Assume full AC. Fix a finite cyclic subdivision of $S^1$ into edges. Let $c:S^1\times(0,1]\to S^2$ be continuous, with each $c_r$ an embedding. On every closed edge require that $c$ extends smoothly to an open neighborhood of that edge times each compact positive-radius interval, and has nonzero edge tangent there. At each subdivision vertex require the two one-sided tangent lines of $c_r$ to be distinct for every $r>0$; the family is smooth away from these finitely many corners. Then
$$D=\{0\}\cup\{r c_r(s):s\in S^1,\ 0<r\le1\}$$
forms a standard ball-disk pair: there is a homeomorphism $(B^3,D)\cong(B^3,B^3\cap\{z=0\})$. In particular it is a properly embedded locally flat closed topological disk. There need be no positive lower bound on corner angles as $r\downarrow0$.

More precisely a radius-preserving homeomorphism of $B^3$ carries $D$ to a disk supplied by a smooth positive-radius family of embedded circles. If the subdivision has no corners and the family is already smooth, this preliminary homeomorphism may be the identity.

Assume full AC. Let $B$ be a smoothly parametrized closed three-ball in a smooth three-manifold. Let $D\subset B$ be a properly embedded locally flat topological disk supplied with a homeomorphism of pairs $(B,D)\cong(B^3,D^2_0)$, where $D^2_0=B^3\cap\{z=0\}$. Suppose $C=\partial D$ is smooth and $D$ is a smooth embedded surface in a neighborhood of $C$, transverse to $\partial B$ there.

There is a smooth properly embedded disk $D'\subset B$, agreeing with $D$ on a smaller boundary collar, and an ambient topological isotopy of $B$, fixed pointwise on $\partial B$, carrying $D$ to $D'$. This isotopy extends by the identity outside $B$. No smoothness or differentiability of the supplied standard-pair homeomorphism is assumed. The assertion requires the actual smooth transverse collar; it does not apply directly to a disk with unrounded corners on its boundary.

Assume full AC. Let $S$ be a compact embedded topological surface in an oriented smooth three-manifold. Suppose it is smooth outside finitely many pairwise disjoint smoothly parametrized seam circles or compact seam arcs, all contained in the interior of $S$. Near each seam it is the union of two supplied smooth embedded half-surfaces meeting precisely in that seam; their inward transverse tangent rays are distinct at every seam point. For an arc, both half-surfaces extend smoothly slightly past its end parameters, and the union $S$ is already smooth on a neighborhood of the two ends. Let $K\subset S$ be a compact set on a neighborhood of which $S$ is smooth.

In any prescribed neighborhood of the nonsmooth locus there is an ambient homeomorphism, supported in that neighborhood and fixed on a neighborhood of $K$, carrying $S$ to a smooth embedded surface. It can be joined to the identity through ambient homeomorphisms with those same support and fixed-set properties. This preserves the surface's homeomorphism type. Distinct rays may be opposite, in which case the surface may already be smooth; they must not coincide. No triangulation or general locally-flat surface smoothing theorem is assumed.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. A compact $C^2$ surface, with regular $C^2$ boundary allowed, is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to a compact smooth surface with smooth boundary. For a compact cooriented embedded surface in a smooth three-manifold, the diffeomorphism can be obtained by arbitrarily small local ambient displacements. This also applies to a compact intrinsic subsurface of a $C^2$ leaf: compactness is in the leaf topology, and its boundary is regular in that topology.

A connected oriented closed such surface with Euler characteristic zero is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $T^2$. A compact regular surface region homeomorphic to a closed disk is $C^2$ diffeomorphic to $D^2$, and any prescribed $C^2$ diffeomorphism of its boundary circle can be realized by the disk parametrization.

Two disjoint regular closed disk regions in a $C^2$ sphere can simultaneously be carried to the standard two disk windows by a $C^2$ diffeomorphism, with compatible prescribed boundary parametrizations. A $C^2$ scalar function defined on a neighborhood of a compact set in $\mathbb R^2$ admits smooth approximations uniformly with its derivatives through order two on that compact set.

Finally let $L$ be a $C^2$ surface and $u:D^2\to L$ an **intrinsically continuous** map which is $C^2$ on an open boundary collar. On any smaller closed boundary collar contained in that open collar, $u$ has arbitrarily close $C^2$ approximations agreeing with $u$ on a neighborhood of the smaller collar, and a homotopy to each approximation fixed there. Closeness is uniform for any fixed compatible metric on $L$. No injectivity or immersion of the cap map is required.

derivations.claim: Choose pairwise disjoint adapted standard-arc charts and outer ellipsoid balls $B_j\subset N$ by [F3]. In each of these same charts perform the collapse [F2], rather than a collapse that only fixes the outer boundary pointwise. Their finite composition $q$ is a smooth diffeomorphism off the union of the arcs, is the identity on neighborhoods of the outer ball boundaries and outside these balls, and has exactly the stated arc fibers. In a sufficiently small target ellipsoid, its level semiaxes are $a\rho,\rho,\rho$. After a fixed diagonal rescaling these are round radius levels. On each source level the actual surface circle in [F3] maps by an invertible diagonal linear map to that target level. Thus in this inner homothetic region its whole surface image is exactly a four-edge radial circle family satisfying [F4]. In particular its restriction to any smaller concentric target ball there is a standard ball-disk pair.

Within each homothetic region choose one smaller target ball $C_j$ and a surrounding annulus still strictly inside that region. Use the explicit [F4] maps there, multiplying their displacements by a radial cutoff equal to one near $\partial C_j$ and zero near both ends of the annulus. The bound in [F4] makes every fiber map an increasing homeomorphism with continuous inverse, so the radius-preserving map $T_j(r\omega)=rT_{j,r}(\omega)$ extends by the identity off the annulus. Near $\partial C_j$ the surface image is a smooth annulus $r\gamma_r(s)$ transverse to the radius spheres, because its radial derivative has radial component one and its regular circle derivative has radial component zero. The map preserves $C_j$, so the disk inside retains a standard-pair chart. Apply [F5] there and extend its boundary-fixed endpoint homeomorphism by the identity. The resulting local homeomorphism $H_j$ is supported inside $B_j$; its surface image is a smooth disk throughout $C_j$ and agrees smoothly with the just constructed annulus on an open boundary collar. These finite supports are disjoint.

Verify the remaining seams before using [F6]. Outside the corner-rounding annuli and inner caps, $q$ is a smooth diffeomorphism and the only surface seams are the images of $L$ minus finitely many intervals. The original radial collar rays there are distinct: coincident rays would give an extra common radial segment, contradicting the specified full intersection set. An invertible smooth derivative preserves distinct inward rays. In a corner annulus the two actual half-sheet images have graph equation $f_r(x)+\lambda(r)\zeta(x)(f_r^\epsilon(x)-f_r(x))$, with the original corner at $x=0$. On each side this is a smooth graph up to $x=0$, and the image seam itself is the smooth curve with graph value $\lambda(r)f_r^\epsilon(0)$. The two outgoing transverse tangents have respectively positive and negative $x$ components, so are distinct for every cutoff value, even where their tangent planes agree. The maps are the identity near annulus support ends, so these descriptions join smoothly to the original seam curves.

Trim each seam inside a smaller collar where the disk cap already agrees with the smooth annulus. The remaining seams are finitely many disjoint smooth compact arcs and circles: the compact smooth link has finitely many components, each inner level sphere meets its image in exactly the four corner points of the level description [F3], and all modifications above are injective away from the original collapsed arcs. Each trimmed arc ends in the smooth annular collar. Its two labeled half-sheets, inherited from $F_0,F_1$ outside the cap, extend geometrically slightly past the end within that unchanged smooth surface collar. One uses the smooth graph and its corner-curve continuation there to divide the collar into two halves; these need not be the images of the originally marked half-sheets inside the cap. Their inward rays remain distinct by step 3.1. All points outside these seams are smooth: the collapse is a diffeomorphism there including near the outer ball boundaries; the annular modifications are smooth on each open half-sheet; the caps and their attaching collars are smooth. Apply [F6] to these actual finite seam data, protecting smaller compact cap disks and taking support inside $N$. Let $R$ be the resulting ambient homeomorphism. Then $Q=R\circ(\prod_jH_j)\circ q$ has exactly the original arc fibers, is fixed off $N$, and its surface image is smooth everywhere.

It remains to identify the smooth components without assuming that smoothing preserves any unspecified model. Take $q_0$ from [F1]. The maps $q_0$ and $q$ have precisely the same fibers on $S^3$. Thus $q$ factors through $q_0$ as a bijection $J:S^3\to S^3$. It is continuous because a continuous surjection from a compact space onto a Hausdorff space is a quotient map. A continuous bijection from compact to Hausdorff is a homeomorphism, so $J$ is an ambient homeomorphism and carries $q_0(F_0\cup F_1)$ onto $q(F_0\cup F_1)$. Composing with the homeomorphisms in step 4.1 shows that the smooth image consists of exactly the same $p$ topological sphere components, with the same assignment of one component from each $F_i$. For an actual smooth sphere parameter, apply the finite smooth handle construction [F7] to each such component. Its Euler characteristic two and its normalized one zero-disk and one two-disk give $2=1-h_1+1$, hence no remaining bands. It is therefore two smooth disks joined along a smooth circle map; extending that map across one disk by [F7], with the transported product collars, identifies it smoothly with the standard sphere. If no arcs occur, use the identity collapse, omit the balls and caps, and round only the distinct radial-collar seams by [F6]; the same count and quotient comparison apply.

boundaries.evidence: Step 5.1 explicitly permits the empty arc list, using identity collapse and only seam rounding.
Step 1.1 collapses zero-radius arc cores using the explicit continuous supplier; no derivative at a collapsed point is claimed.
Step 5.1 includes p=1 and arbitrary finite arc count.
Step 3.1 verifies distinct transverse rays even when tangent planes agree in the smoothed annulus; positive and negative x components prevent cusp degeneration.
Step 4.1 extends seam halves geometrically into a protected smooth collar, without asserting smoothness of the marked quotient graph inside the cap.
The Statement assumes full AC inherited from sphere count and smoothing suppliers; Step 1.1 through Step 4.1 use finite disjoint supports.

axioms.use: Full AC is inherited from the finite balanced-surface sphere count, parametric corner rounding and relative smooth cap suppliers. Only finitely many arcs, balls, annuli and seam components are used.

risk_review.notes: All actual seam hypotheses are verified. The marked graph Q(L) is not claimed smooth inside the cap, and no diagram reconstruction/nonsplit connectivity/full flyping conclusion is inferred. Smooth sphere parameters use the actual finite smooth handle normal form, not uniqueness of smooth structures without proof.

contract.proof_status_evidence: Five complete local proof rows with scoped final checks. Root mathematical acceptance and canonical readiness remain pending.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 Choose a proper strip around $A$ on $F_0$. Explicitly take a smooth transverse field along that interval, tangent to $L$ at its ends, extend it in finitely many surface charts tangent to the boundary, and use its short flow in [F1]. Normalize its restriction at each end to the unit boundary tangent, with whichever sign is continuous along the strip. Its flow coordinates give $c_0(x,y)$, $-1\le x\le1$, $|y|<\delta$, with $c_0(x,0)=A(x)$ and with the two end edges on $L$. Extend this map slightly across its end faces in the original smooth boundary charts, patching extensions off the prescribed strip if necessary. The strip is orientable, so its two tangent vectors define a smooth unit ambient normal. Its short normal exponential map gives a smooth ambient chart $(x,y,z)$ by [F1] and compact injectivity, with $F_0$ given by $z=0$, $-1\le x\le1$, and the two short pieces of $L$ by $x=\pm1,z=0$. The chart can be taken inside $U$, missing every other sheet of either embedded surface; locally these are the given surface charts, and compactness of the arc supplies a common sufficiently small width. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 On $F_1$ near $A$, the ambient coordinate $x$ is a submersion, since its derivative on $\dot A$ is one. Choose a nonzero smooth field in its one-dimensional kernel along $A$, and extend it nearby while retaining $dx=0$. One obtains this by subtracting the $x$ component with a local field having $dx=1$, then patching the kernel fields in finitely many charts, close enough to their fixed nonzero values along $A$. At the two end edges the kernel is exactly tangent to $L$, so choose its boundary value to be $\sigma_\pm\partial_y$, $\sigma_\pm\in\{1,-1\}$, with the sign continuous from the interior. Its flow from [F1] gives an actual parametrization $c_1(x,t)=(x,Y(x,t),Z(x,t))$, with $(Y,Z)(x,0)=0$ and with $Y(\pm1,t)=\sigma_\pm t$, $Z(\pm1,t)=0$. The two transverse derivatives $(Y_t,Z_t)$ are never simultaneously zero along the compact arc. The formula $v(x,t)=\int_0^1(Y_t,Z_t)(x,ut)\,du$ gives $(Y,Z)=t\,v(x,t)$ with smooth $v$ and $|v|>0$ on a uniform smaller strip. Thus its normal radius is $R(x,t)=|t|a(x,t)$ for smooth $a=|v|>0$, and shrinking makes $a+t a_t>0$ uniformly. It is strictly increasing on each positive transverse half and strictly decreasing on each negative half. [step 1.1, F1, construct, algebra]

3.1 Take the closed confocal ellipsoids $E_\rho=\{x^2/(1+\rho^2)+(y^2+z^2)/\rho^2\le1\}$ for $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$, choosing $\varepsilon$ sufficiently small with strict margins inside the chart and the two strips. On either surface a point of $\partial E_\rho$ with axial coordinate $x\in[-1,1]$ has normal radius $R_\rho(x)=\rho\sqrt{1-x^2/(1+\rho^2)}>0$. By step 2.1, for each $x$ there is exactly one point of each transverse half of $F_1$ at this radius. For $F_0$ the two points are simply $y=\pm R_\rho(x),z=0$. Existence is uniform because $R_\rho\le\rho$ and the radii at the two fixed outer strip edges have a positive common lower bound. The implicit inverse in [F1] shows that these four edges, parametrized by $x\in[-1,1]$, depend smoothly on $x,\rho$ for $\rho>0$, including their endpoints; each is regular since its first coordinate is $x$. There are no surface points with $x$ beyond these end faces in this neighborhood: both surfaces have boundary exactly on those faces and point inward along $A$. [step 1.1, step 2.1, F1, construct, algebra]

4.1 At $x=\pm1$ the radius is $\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2}$. Hence the four edge ends lie at the two points $y=\pm\rho^2/\sqrt{1+\rho^2},z=0$ on each end piece of $L$, with the same page pairings as in [F2]. Distinct pairings make their union $C_\rho$ one embedded circle. Its four corners have distinct tangent lines. Indeed boundary-curve transversality at the original arc endpoints says that the difference of the two radial angle functions has nonzero derivative there. For sufficiently small nonzero displacement along $L$, their angle difference is nonzero modulo $\pi$, so the two surface tangent planes at each of these corner points are distinct, meeting exactly in $TL$. Also $L$ is transverse to $\partial E_\rho$: its coordinate tangent is $\partial_y$ and the derivative of the ellipsoid equation in that direction is $2y/\rho^2\ne0$. If the two edge tangent lines on the ellipsoid agreed, that common line would lie in $TL\cap T\partial E_\rho=0$, a contradiction. This proves the required corner independence for every $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$ after shrinking once. The strict margins also permit a short extension past the outer radius. [step 3.1, F1, F2, construct, contradiction]

5.1 Use the actual confocal-ellipsoid collapse of [F3] in this adapted chart. It fixes $\partial E_\varepsilon$ and the outside, collapses exactly $A$, and sends $E_\rho$ to $(\rho/\varepsilon)E_\varepsilon$. On each positive level its restriction is the invertible linear map $(x,y,z)\mapsto(\rho\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}\,x/(\varepsilon\sqrt{1+\rho^2}),y,z)$. Therefore it carries the four edges of $C_\rho$ to a regular four-edge circle with the same distinct corner tangent lines and smooth dependence on every positive $\rho$. Apply the fixed diagonal linear rescaling $E_\varepsilon\to B^3$ and put $r=\rho/\varepsilon$. These image circles are now exactly a finite-corner radial family satisfying [F4]; their cyclic edge ordering is fixed by the two end matchings and does not change with radius. [step 3.1, step 4.1, F3, construct, algebra]

6.1 Let $K=(F_0\cup F_1)\cap E_\varepsilon$. The level description in step 3.1 shows that it consists exactly of $A$ and the circles $C_\rho$, $0<\rho\le\varepsilon$. Thus after the collapse and diagonal rescaling its entire image, not just selected levels, is the radial disk in [F4]. That supplier gives a homeomorphism of the ball-disk pair to the standard pair. Pull back the diagonal rescaling to conclude that $(E_\varepsilon,q(K))$ is a standard ball-disk pair. Set $B$ to be this ellipsoid in the original ambient chart and extend the collapse by the identity outside it, as in [F3]. It is supported in $U$, has just $A$ as a nonsingleton fiber, and maps $B$ to itself. This proves the local flatness and all asserted support and fiber properties. Every construction used only the two local strips, so neither connectedness nor orientability of the complete surfaces was required. [step 3.1, step 5.1, F3, F4, construct] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual Proof 3.1–6.1 supplies four regular level edges, distinct corner lines, exact coverage, and four boundary-link corner points on each level.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 At a corner let $a_r,b_r$ be the two unit tangent rays pointing away from that vertex along the incident edges. They depend smoothly on $r>0$ and are linearly independent. In the tangent plane choose the unit $x$ direction parallel to $b_r-a_r$, and the $y$ direction its positive quarter-turn. The two rays have strictly negative and positive $x$ components respectively, since $a_r\cdot(b_r-a_r)=a_r\cdot b_r-1<0$ and $b_r\cdot(b_r-a_r)=1-a_r\cdot b_r>0$. Smooth sphere exponential coordinates in that frame, followed by [F2] on each branch, therefore make the incident curve a graph $y=f_r(x)$, with $f_r(0)=0$, smooth on either side of zero and continuous at zero. The graph chart and its inverse vary smoothly with $r$ on each branch. The corner points, the other parts of the curve and a chosen midpoint of one edge are distinct, so compactness on every closed positive-radius interval permits disjoint corner boxes avoiding that marked midpoint and all other curve pieces. [given, F2, construct, algebra]

2.1 Choose positive smooth functions $\rho(r),\kappa(r)$ so that the graph exists for $|x|<\kappa(r)$ and the coordinate box $|x|<\kappa(r),|y|<\rho(r)$ has the separation properties of step 1.1; these two functions may be taken equal to one common valid square-size bound. Here and below these functions are obtained by first taking lower chart-size bounds on each compact interval $[2^{-n-2},2^{-n+1}]\cap(0,1]$, selecting this countable list under full AC, and using a smooth locally finite partition of the radius interval subordinate to their interiors. A weighted average of valid smaller lower bounds is valid, since each active bound is valid at that radius and the conditions persist on shrinking. Such a partition is given by positive bumps divided by their locally finite positive sum. Choose $a(r)<\rho(r)/10$. On $|x|\le\kappa(r)/2$, choose a positive smooth upper bound $M(r)$ for both branch slopes by the same compact-interval method; weighted averages of valid upper bounds remain upper bounds. Set $h(r)=(10/\kappa(r)+100(1+M(r))/a(r))^{-1}$. Then $3h<\kappa/2$ and $|f_r(x)|\le M|x|<a/4$ for $|x|<3h$. Thus the larger box $|x|<3h,|y|<3a$ stays inside the chart, and the finite corner supports remain disjoint and avoid the marked midpoint. Near radius one use a short extension of the given smooth data. All choices have been made on positive radii; no uniform bound at zero is used. [step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix a nonnegative smooth kernel $\eta$ supported in $[-1,1]$ with integral one, for example the normalized function $\exp(-1/(1-t^2))$ there. For a positive smooth $\epsilon(r)<h(r)$ define $f_r^\epsilon(x)=\int_{-1}^1 f_r(x-\epsilon(r)t)\eta(t)\,dt$ on $|x|<2h(r)$. If $M(r)$ bounds the two branch slopes, then $|f_r^\epsilon-f_r|\le M(r)\epsilon(r)$. The convolved function is smooth jointly in $r,x$ across zero: rewrite the integral with its smooth translated kernel and split the integration over the two sides of the fixed corner; on a compact radius interval all derivatives on each side are bounded, so differentiation under these finite integrals is valid. Let $\chi$ be smooth, equal to one on $[-1/3,1/3]$ and zero outside $(-1,1)$. Put $g_r=f_r+\chi(x/h(r))(f_r^\epsilon-f_r)$ and $\Delta_r=g_r-f_r$. Then $g_r$ is smooth across zero and equals $f_r$ off $|x|<h(r)$. Choose $\epsilon(r)$ small enough that $|\Delta_r|<a(r)/(10(1+\|\chi'\|_\infty))$; the bounds from step 2.1 allow a positive smooth such choice. [step 2.1, construct, algebra]

4.1 In this corner box use the fiber map $T_r(x,y)=(x,y+\chi((y-f_r(x))/a(r))\Delta_r(x))$. It sends the graph of $f_r$ to that of $g_r$. Its derivative in $y$ is $1+\chi'((y-f_r(x))/a(r))\Delta_r(x)/a(r)>1/2$. For each fixed $x$ it is therefore an increasing homeomorphism of the vertical interval, equal to the identity near its ends; outside the horizontal support it is the identity too. Thus it is a homeomorphism of the box, and extending by the identity gives a sphere homeomorphism. It depends continuously on $r$, as does its inverse: strict monotonicity with this lower slope bound gives continuous inverses in the vertical coordinate, and the moving chart coordinates are smooth. The nonsmooth $f_r$ in this formula is harmless, since only a homeomorphism is required. Compose over the finitely many disjoint corner boxes. The resulting sphere homeomorphisms $T_r$ and their inverses vary continuously for $r>0$ and carry each original circle to a smooth embedded circle $\Gamma_r$. [step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 These smoothed circles admit a smooth parametrization on $S^1\times(0,1]$. Start at the marked midpoint retained in step 1.1, orient by the original cyclic edge order, and use normalized arclength. In the corner charts the graphs $g_r$ are jointly smooth; outside them the old edges are jointly smooth, and on the overlap the two descriptions agree. Their speeds are positive, so finite chart integration makes their total length and partial lengths smooth on each compact positive-radius interval. Inverting arclength locally by [F2] gives the claimed joint smooth parametrization, and its definitions agree around the whole circle with total length as period. Finally set $T(0)=0$ and $T(r\omega)=r T_r(\omega)$ on the punctured ball. The inverse has the corresponding formula with $T_r^{-1}$. Both are continuous at zero solely because they preserve radius. Hence $T$ is a ball homeomorphism carrying $D$ to the radial surface of this smooth circle family. Apply [F1] to that surface and compose with $T$. This proves the standard pair and local-flatness conclusions, with no corner-angle limit assumed. In the already smooth case take $T_r$ to be the identity and apply [F1] directly. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F1, F2, construct] ∎
constructive_supplier_evidence.use: Actual Proof 3.1–5.1 supplies the vertical displacement and derivative bound and jointly smooth circle parametrization.

constructive_supplier_evidence.exact_read_body:
1.1 All local selection in the compact constructions below is finite. In a $C^2$ chart choose nested coordinate balls and compose a Euclidean smooth bump with the chart; extension by zero gives a $C^2$ bump with support in that chart. Finite compact-core covers and normalization by the positive finite sum give $C^2$ partitions. In a smooth ambient manifold the same construction gives smooth bumps and partitions near a compact set. For a compact abstract $C^2$ surface $S$, choose finitely many such charts $x_i$ and bumps $b_i$ whose positive sets cover $S$. The map $J=(b_i,b_ix_i)_i$, extending each block by zero, is a $C^2$ embedding into a finite-dimensional Euclidean space: equality of the $b_i$ blocks and any positive $b_i$ recovers equality of $x_i$, hence of the points. If $dJ(v)=0$, then $db_i(v)=0$ and $b_i dx_i(v)=0$ for a positive block, hence $v=0$. A continuous injective map from compact $S$ to a Hausdorff space has continuous inverse on its image; the local inverse in chart projections is $C^2$ by [F1]. Half-space charts give the same argument at the boundary. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 First treat a closed cooriented embedded hypersurface $S$ in a smooth three-manifold. In finitely many ambient neighborhoods take $C^2$ defining functions $F_i$, zero precisely on $S$ there, with their differentials positive on the chosen common normal side. Multiply by an ambient smooth partition $\rho_i$ whose sum is one near $S$ and put $F=\sum_i\rho_iF_i$. On $S$, $dF=\sum_i\rho_i dF_i$, because $F_i=0$ kills every term $F_i d\rho_i$; this differential is nonzero and positively normal. Local implicit uniqueness and a finite shrinking therefore give a neighborhood of $S$ on which $F^{-1}(0)=S$. Positive local smooth transverse vectors, shrunk so they remain positive, glue by smooth nonnegative weights to a smooth field $V$ with $dF(V)>0$ near $S$. Finite coordinate convolutions and an ambient smooth partition, using [F2], give a smooth $G$ arbitrarily close to $F$ in $C^2$ on a compact smaller neighborhood. [F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Write $\Phi_t$ for the smooth flow of $V$. Compactness gives a uniform short flow strip on which $dF(V)>c>0$; the map $(x,t)\mapsto\Phi_t(x)$ is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism on a smaller strip about $S$. Its differential is invertible on the zero section; if no uniform injective strip existed, coincident points in successively thinner strips would have convergent base points, their limits would coincide, and local injectivity at that point would contradict the coincidences. For $G$ sufficiently close, $dG(V)>c/2$ and $G$ has opposite signs at the strip ends. Thus $G(\Phi_t(x))=0$ has a unique root $t=\tau(x)$, $C^2$ by [F1]. The map $x\mapsto\Phi_{\tau(x)}(x)$ identifies $S$ with the smooth level in that strip. Its $C^2$ inverse is obtained by the unique root of $F=0$ on the same flow orbit. A time cutoff extends the displacement to a $C^2$ ambient diffeomorphism supported in the strip: in these coordinates use $(x,t)\mapsto(x,t+\eta(t)\tau(x))$; choosing the approximation small makes $1+\eta'(t)\tau(x)>0$. [F1, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The abstract embedding in step 1.1 can have higher codimension; a scalar defining function is not asserted for it. Here is the needed finite replacement. A $C^2$ embedded surface is locally a graph $v=h(z)$ over a fixed two-plane by [F1]. On a compact graph patch replace $h$ by a smooth $h'$ arbitrarily close in $C^2$, and use the ambient map $(z,v)\mapsto(z,v+\eta(z,v)(h'(z)-h(z)))$, with a smooth compactly supported $\eta$ equal to one near the compact graph core. If the difference is sufficiently small in $C^1$, this is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism: its difference from the identity has derivative norm less than one, which proves injectivity by the mean-value estimate, and the local inverse is $C^2$; compact support gives surjectivity. The moved surface is a smooth graph near that core. To preserve already smoothed compact cores $K$, take $h'=h$ near their projections wherever the patch meets $K$. Such projections have an open neighborhood where $h$ is smooth. A smooth cutoff $\mu$, supported in that neighborhood and one near the relevant compact projections, gives $h'=\mu h+(1-\mu)h_\epsilon$, which is smooth and $C^2$ close to $h$. Cut the ambient support away from any other protected cores. The displacement is then the identity near $K$. [step 3.1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct]

5.1 Choose compact chart cores covering the original surface. Carry those cores and the remaining graph neighborhoods along each displacement. Apply step 4.1 successively to the finitely many cores, with the union of the earlier moved cores protected. Compactness allows finite refinements into graph patches and arbitrarily small displacements so that all needed graph projections remain regular. After the last patch the image is smooth near every core, hence everywhere. For boundary charts, extend the local graph $C^2$ across its half-plane boundary before convolution; the definition of $C^2$ regularity in a boundary chart supplies precisely such local extensions. This initially smooths the underlying surface graph, leaving a regular $C^2$ boundary curve in those smooth graph coordinates. Apply the same finite graph displacement argument, now to one-dimensional boundary graphs within these smooth surface coordinates, relative to previously smoothed boundary cores. Its coordinate displacements are $C^2$, have support in these patches, and smooth the boundary; every boundary core then has a smooth half-space chart. This proves the abstract assertion without an atlas-smoothing theorem. [F1, F2, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 For an actual cooriented surface region with boundary, one can retain the normal-root construction. Extend its local surface graphs across the regular boundary and apply step 2.1 on a finite neighborhood of the region; at the boundary the extensions agree on the interior side, which is all that is needed for the root projection of the region itself. The moved region lies in smooth local surface graphs and has $C^2$ boundary. Alternatively step 5.1 provides an unambiguous finite ambient construction there. On the smooth underlying surface near the boundary, take a $C^2$ signed boundary defining function $H$ using finitely many boundary graph charts and smooth weights; its inward differential is nonzero. Smooth it to $H'$ and take a smooth inward-transverse surface field $W$. The equations $H'(\Psi_t(y))=0$, with $y$ on the old boundary, give a $C^2$ boundary displacement with inverse obtained from $H=0$. Extend it with a cutoff in its flow collar exactly as in step 3.1. This maps the region to a smooth-boundary region. A compact intrinsic leaf subsurface has embedded ambient inclusion: the leaf inclusion is an injective immersion, and its restriction to a compact intrinsic subsurface is a homeomorphism onto its image by compactness and Hausdorffness. The above finite construction therefore applies; other, possibly dense, parts of that leaf are not part of this carrier. [F1, F2, step 3.1, step 5.1, construct]

7.1 Let $\psi:S^1\to S^1$ be an orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphism. Its increasing $C^2$ lift $a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ satisfies $a(\theta+2\pi)=a(\theta)+2\pi$ and $a'>0$. Choose a smooth radial cutoff $\beta$ zero near $r=0$ and one near $r=1$. In polar coordinates put $E(r,\theta)=(r,\theta+\beta(r)(a(\theta)-\theta))$. Periodicity makes this well-defined, and its angular derivative $1-\beta(r)+\beta(r)a'(\theta)$ is positive. Thus each circle map is bijective; [F1] gives a $C^2$ inverse on the annulus, and $E$ is the identity near the origin. This is a $C^2$ disk diffeomorphism restricting to $\psi$, with product collar expression near the boundary. For an orientation-reversing map first compose with the fixed reflection of the disk. The same formula is smooth for smooth data. [step 6.1, F1, construct]

8.1 We give the smooth normal-form argument explicitly. Apply [F4] to the smoothed surface with empty incoming face and boundary as outgoing face; use both faces empty in the closed case. Obtain finitely many disks (zero-handles), rectangles (one-handles) and capping disks (two-handles), with all zeros before ones before twos. Before forming the graph, transport any attaching windows on earlier rectangles back to zero-disk boundary arcs: along a rectangle side use its product collar, move the finite windows in order to its endpoint collar, and continue onto the zero-disk boundary, shrinking windows to leave disjoint gaps. For an increasing interval map $f$ fixed at the endpoints, the collar map $(s,t)\mapsto((1-\alpha(t))s+\alpha(t)f(s),t)$ has positive first derivative; successive such maps give each transport and carry the affected band with it. Induction over the finitely many bands gives a presentation with every band attached to disjoint intervals of zero-disks. Its core is then an edge between the zero-disks. The resulting graph is connected when the surface is: each capping disk attaches along a connected circle and cannot join two components. Choose a finite spanning tree. The union of its disks and bands is diffeomorphic to a disk, by successive leaf disk-and-band absorptions described next. Every other attaching interval is transported in these absorptions, rather than discarded. [step 7.1, F4, construct]

9.1 For the absorption move, two disks joined along a single band are a disk after rounding their four corners: straighten the two attaching intervals in boundary collar coordinates, rescale the band's product coordinates to a rectangle, and identify the resulting union with a planar rounded disk-and-rectangle model. Its boundary is parametrized by the successive arcs and the two sides of the rectangle; a collar of that boundary and radial coordinates on a smaller interior disk give the usual disk parametrization. More explicitly one may straighten the disks into end caps of the rectangle and choose the rounded union to be a convex stadium, hence star-shaped about its midpoint; its radial boundary function is positive and smooth, and radial rescaling, cut off to a constant linear rescaling near the center, identifies it with a round disk. Boundary arc parametrizations are transported by increasing interval maps. If attaching windows of other bands lie on the absorbed disk, they remain disjoint ordered intervals on the new disk boundary. To put them in prescribed positions choose an increasing boundary map with the prescribed maps on those finitely many disjoint intervals; on the complementary intervals interpolate positive derivatives with the required integral. On a boundary rectangle $(s,t)$ extend its isotopy by $(s,t)\mapsto((1-\alpha(t))s+\alpha(t)f(s),t)$, with the interval endpoints fixed and $\alpha$ zero at the inner edge. Its Jacobian in the $s$ direction is positive. Composing finitely many such collar maps transports all attaching windows and their band coordinates. This is the explicit surface handle slide/straightening needed for each tree contraction; it invokes no higher-dimensional handle-slide theorem. [step 8.1, construct]

10.1 After primal contractions there is one zero-disk. View the same presentation upside down: a two-disk is a dual zero-disk, a rectangle is a dual rectangle with its factors interchanged, and the zero-disk is a dual capping disk. The dual graph is connected by the same connectedness argument. A dual spanning tree and the absorptions of step 9.1 leave one dual zero-disk, hence one original two-disk. Transport later attachments at every contraction by the same rectangle collar maps. These operations are actual diffeomorphisms of the entire surface: the disk-plus-band replacements agree on the boundary collars used to attach the rest. Each primal contraction decreases $h_0,h_1$ by one, and each dual contraction decreases $h_1,h_2$ by one. If $\chi=0$, [F4] now gives $0=1-h_1+1$, hence precisely two remaining bands. This calculation concerns the actual Morse handles, regardless of how many cells were present in any original topological cellulation. [F4, step 8.1, step 9.1, construct]

11.1 Orientability forbids a twisted band. The first untwisted band on the remaining disk gives an annulus: straighten its two windows by the collar maps in step 9.1; the standard disk with that rectangle is the planar annulus. The second band must join its two boundary circles. Indeed, attachment to intervals on the same boundary circle of an oriented annulus increases the number of boundary components to three, whereas joining the two circles leaves one, and the single final two-disk can cap only one circle. Straighten the two windows on the different annulus circles and extend their boundary maps over disjoint collars. An interval attaching map has no additional twist once the surface orientation is fixed; positive changes of its longitudinal parameter extend across the rectangle by the positive-derivative interpolation in step 9.1. Thus this is the standard annulus with one joining band, a once-punctured torus. Its remaining boundary is a circle; a circle attaching diffeomorphism extends over the final disk by step 7.1. Capping therefore gives the standard torus. Composing with the carrier diffeomorphism proves the $C^2$ torus assertion. [F4, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, construct]

12.1 For a smooth region homeomorphic to a disk, cap its outgoing boundary with an auxiliary disk and mark that disk as an exterior dual vertex. A smooth circle parametrization needed for the cap is obtained by ordering finitely many regular curve charts around the circle and choosing a positive smooth speed on their overlaps. First contract the primal tree as above. The capped surface's dual graph is connected; choose a spanning tree rooted at the marked exterior vertex. Successively absorb the other dual disks towards that root using step 9.1. In original coordinates this deletes an internal two-disk together with a band; the exterior disk is not deleted, and its boundary collar is transported, so removing it at the end gives a diffeomorphism of the original region. There remain one zero-disk, no two-disks and $h_1$ bands. Its Euler characteristic is one, since it is homeomorphic to a disk, so [F4] gives $1=1-h_1$, hence $h_1=0$. The region is therefore a smooth disk, by an actual composition of disk/band collar moves. Pulling back by step 5.1 gives a $C^2$ parametrization of the original disk region; composing with the extension in step 7.1 realizes any prescribed boundary parametrization. [step 11.1, F4, step 5.1, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, construct]

13.1 For completeness, an oriented compact annulus has a disk-and-band normal form by the same moves. Cap both boundary circles with marked exterior disks, contract the primal tree, and contract a dual forest rooted at those exterior disks (one root for each component of the forest). Every internal dual disk is absorbed into a root, so in the original annulus no internal two-disk remains. There is one zero-disk and, by $\chi=0$, one band. Orientability and the two boundary components make this the standard untwisted annulus. For two disjoint regular disks in a $C^2$ sphere, first smooth the sphere and then both marked boundary curves by the boundary moves in step 6.1, transporting the disks. Choose a common signed transverse-flow collar of each resulting smooth boundary curve. All disk-and-band moves can use these supplied collars: their interval maps extend as product maps on smaller collars and are cut off farther inside by the positive-derivative interpolation of step 9.1. For these disks their complement is connected with two boundary circles and Euler characteristic zero: paths can be rerouted around each removed disk along its boundary collar, and capping these two boundary circles recovers the sphere. The preceding normal form identifies this complement with an annulus. Given compatible boundary parametrizations, their increasing angle lifts $a_0,a_1$ extend across it by $a_t=(1-\lambda(t))a_0+\lambda(t)a_1$, with $\lambda$ constant near both ends; the angular derivative is positive. Parametrize the two disks by step 12.1 with those same collars, and use the constant-end interpolation on the annulus with the common signed collar coordinate. The maps on the two sides thus have identical product expressions on a whole seam neighborhood, so gluing is a $C^2$ diffeomorphism. This gives the simultaneous sphere diffeomorphism and prescribed windows. The scalar approximation assertion is [F2], after extending the function by a cutoff equal to one near its compact set and convolving. [F2, step 7.1, step 9.1, step 10.1, step 12.1, construct]

14.1 Let $K=u(D^2)$, compact in the intrinsic topology. Choose finitely many precompact leaf charts with $C^2$ bumps $b_i$ positive on $K$, as in step 1.1. Their sum $b$ has compact support in $L$ and a positive minimum on $K$. Take a regular value $c$ strictly between zero and that minimum: cover the compact support by finitely many charts and apply [F3], so the finite union of bad value sets is null and cannot fill this interval. Then $P=\{b\ge c\}$ is a compact intrinsic $C^2$ subsurface with regular boundary and contains $K$ in its interior. Step 5.1 supplies a $C^2$ diffeomorphism $q:P\to P'$ with $P'$ smooth. Glue two copies of $P'$ along a smooth boundary collar to obtain its compact smooth double $Q$; collars can be read in the finite smooth boundary charts, gluing their inward fields by a finite smooth partition and taking their smooth flow. Thus $q(K)$ lies in the interior of the designated copy of $P'$ in the boundaryless smooth carrier $Q$. [step 13.1, F1, F3, step 1.1, step 5.1, construct]

15.1 By [F5] smoothly embed $Q$ into $\mathbb R^N$, writing $j$ for the embedding, and take a smooth retraction $R$ from a tubular neighborhood onto $j(Q)$. Let $v=jqu$. This is continuous on the disk and $C^2$ on the given open collar. Extend it continuously across the disk boundary by its boundary values constant on short radial rays, and multiply outside a larger disk by a continuous compact-support cutoff. Euclidean convolution gives smooth maps $v_\epsilon$ uniformly approaching $v$ on $D^2$ by [F2]. Choose a smooth scalar cutoff $\gamma$ equal to zero near the specified smaller collar and equal to one off a slightly larger collar whose closure still lies in the original $C^2$ collar. Set $w_\epsilon=v+\gamma(v_\epsilon-v)$. Where $\gamma\ne1$, the original $v$ is $C^2$; where $v$ is only continuous, $\gamma=1$ on a neighborhood and $w_\epsilon=v_\epsilon$. Thus $w_\epsilon$ is $C^2$ everywhere and equals $v$ near the smaller collar. [F2, F5, step 14.1, construct]

16.1 The compact set $v(D^2)$ is inside the tubular domain and inside $j(\operatorname{int}P')$. By continuity of $R$ and compactness, sufficiently small uniform perturbations and their entire straight segments from $v$ remain in the tubular domain and retract into $j(\operatorname{int}P')$. Define $u_\epsilon=q^{-1}j^{-1}R(w_\epsilon)$, using $j^{-1}$ on that copy. It is $C^2$, agrees with $u$ near the prescribed smaller collar, and converges uniformly to $u$. The formula $q^{-1}j^{-1}R((1-s)v+sw_\epsilon)$ gives a continuous homotopy fixed there. Uniform convergence in any compatible metric follows from uniform continuity of $q^{-1}j^{-1}R$ near this compact image; no regularity or injectivity of $u$ was used away from its collar. [F5, step 14.1, step 15.1, construct]

17.1 The finite constructions prove the carrier, normal-form and relative approximation assertions. All selections particular to these compact carriers are finite. Countable choice is inherited only from the convolution, smooth-flow, Morse/handle, smooth-embedding and tubular suppliers; no arbitrary-index Axiom of Choice or general $C^2$ atlas-smoothing result is used. [F1, F2, F4, F5, step 6.1, step 11.1, step 12.1, step 16.1] ∎
